meta.title: Check your understanding: Concentrated solar power

objectives: Explain why concentrated solar power needs direct sunlight and how a heliostat aims its reflection
Calculate the Carnot ceiling and the heat stored in a tank of molten salt
Compare stored heat in a CSP plant with photovoltaics for supplying power after sunset

questions.prompt: Why is concentrated solar power (CSP) built almost only in deserts and dry, sunny regions, while solar panels also work under cloud?
choices: Only the direct beam of sunlight can be focused by mirrors, not diffuse light
Mirrors crack in cold, damp weather, so they only last in deserts
The molten salt stays liquid only where the air itself is hot
Deserts get more ultraviolet light, which is what heats the receiver
questions.explain: Mirrors can only focus the beam that casts sharp shadows; the diffuse glow of a cloudy sky arrives from every direction and cannot be concentrated. The salt is kept molten by the collected heat, so warm air is not what decides where CSP is built.

questions.prompt: A CSP plant collects heat at 400 °C and rejects waste heat at 30 °C. What is its Carnot ceiling?
questions.explain: In kelvin, 1 − 303.15 ÷ 673.15 ≈ 0.55, so at most 55 %. 93 % comes from using degrees Celsius, and 64 % is the ceiling for Gemasolar's hotter 565 °C salt: the cooler plant has the lower ceiling, which is why hotter towers can beat troughs.

questions.prompt: A plant holds 500 tonnes of solar salt (specific heat about 1,500 J/(kg·K)) heated from 290 °C to 565 °C. How much heat does it store?
questions.explain: E = 500,000 × 1,500 × 275 ≈ 2.1 × 10¹¹ J, and dividing by 3.6 × 10⁹ gives about 57 MWh of heat. 118 MWh uses 565 °C as the temperature rise instead of the 275 K between the tanks, and 23 MWh is the electricity a 40 % steam cycle would make from that heat, not the heat itself.

questions.prompt: In a power-tower field, how is each heliostat mirror angled?
choices: Straight at the Sun, so it catches as much light as possible
Straight at the tower, so its light is sure to land on the receiver
Flat, so it reflects the same amount of light all day
So that it bisects the angle between the Sun and the receiver
questions.explain: A mirror reflects at equal angles, so to send sunlight to the tower its surface must face halfway between the Sun and the receiver. A mirror pointed straight at the Sun would send the light back towards the Sun, and this halfway rule is why mirrors on the far side of the tower from the Sun face it most squarely.
